Point 7 is the most important, as you allow your champion to share his success with others (and, more importantly, with his boss).

I cannot disclose the number, but we're now entering an era in which large-scale collection matters, and there is NO room for mistakes.
-> Hopefully, we test every AI call, email, and answer BEFORE starting collection, so we never receive any hard disputes or complaints

author.occupation: Founder & CEO – Respaid (YC S23) | Helping B2B companies get paid respectfully

text:
We don't guess what makes people pay. We engineer it.

Most of the industry starts onboarding by asking: "What should we say to your customers? Let's discuss strategy."

What we do differently is using data to determine what people actually respond to. 

We built our entire collection approach on engineering, not artistic way or feelings or experience.

Our system tracks everything:

Which emails get opened 
What device they're reading from (iPhone, Android, desktop) 
Their location 
Exact click behavior

Then we use that data to determine the next move.

If someone opens an email on their phone at 3pm but doesn't click, our AI follows up with a text within the hour.

If they clicked but didn't pay, it triggers a call the next morning.

This lets us move faster.

No need for weeks of strategy discussions or waiting for documentation.

The data tells us exactly what to say, when to say it, and which channel to use.

That's how we hit a 50% collection rate on average within 20 days.

Just engineering and speed.

author.occupation: Founder & CEO – Respaid (YC S23) | Helping B2B companies get paid respectfully

text:
Most companies think the problem is sending MORE reminders.

It's not.

The problem is you're texting the wrong person at the wrong time.

Here's what we learned processing up to 85,000 collections per day:

Email open rate: 78% 
Text message open rate: 98% 

However, the text payment rate is only 12%. 

Why the gap?

Because the person who opens your text (the small business owner rushing between meetings) isn't sitting at their computer ready to approve a wire transfer.

They see it. They think "I'll handle this later." Then they forget.

So we engineered a system that tracks behavior:

If someone opens your text but doesn't pay within 2 hours, we send an email with a one click payment link to their desktop.

Timing is everything.

We track time zones because your 2pm might be their midnight.

We avoid Friday at 6pm when people are leaving the office.

We skip Black Friday when response rates tank.

We monitor email engagement to know their actual location and when they're most likely to act.

This engineering approach helped us achieve up to 50% collection rate on average.

The lesson?

Stop doing more of what doesn't work.

Start doing the right thing at the right time.

author.occupation: Founder & CEO – Respaid (YC S23) | Helping B2B companies get paid respectfully

text:
One Excel file. That's all we need to start.

The standard collection process require documentation, past history, and detailed records upfront. It's a common industry practice that helps build comprehensive cases.

We built a different approach: we only ask for an Excel spreadsheet.

Why? Because we assume your customers already have all those invoices and contracts—they've received them from you in the past.

And if a customer claims they don't have them? Our AI sends a tutorial within minutes showing them exactly how to log into your customer dashboard and retrieve it themselves.

Here's where the real magic happens: we don't just take your spreadsheet, we analyze it.

Missing emails? We find them. Outdated phone numbers? We update them. (Up to 15% of contacts become outdated each year.) Generic contact addresses? We replace them with the actual person who can pay.

This means we reach out smarter, to the right person, before we even start collecting.

That's how we process up to 85,000 collections per day.

text:
I'm deeply optimistic and passionate about the field of AI and actively working to push it forward but I honestly think if you're not a little bit afraid at this moment in tech, you're not really paying attention. And I think that fear is healthy and necessary. 

To be honest, I feel it too. It feels important to admit that. I want to normalize it! It shouldn't be taboo or seen as anti-AI either. In fact, it's what will drive the action we all need to take.

Optimism will help us imagine what a great future could look like.

A healthy skepticism and fear is how we get there through the potential pitfalls.

That's what was on my mind as I planned how to fill 3 hours on BBC Radio 4 for the Today program. Growing up in London, BBC was an institution. So it was a pretty full circle moment for me getting the chance to be a guest editor spot.

I just kept coming back to this idea that tech needs both optimism AND pessimism. We absolutely should be scared of the risks. We absolutely need to be concerned about what could go wrong.

That's what will help it go right.

So I ended up filling the time with stories on climate and energy, AI consciousness (the lack thereof), refugees, and the need for new AI governance. Big thanks to BBC icon Amol Rajan for closing it out by putting me in the interview chair and asking what all this means for the future. Couldn't ask for a better wrap-up or smarter questions. 

You can watch a bit of our conversation here: https://lnkd.in/eNQChZhT

text:
Got to talk about one of my most contrarian takes on the Moonshots podcast: I think the AGI "race" is a huge misnomer.

Yes, labs around the world are going as fast as they can to invent better and better models.

But a race implies there is one finish line and one (maybe two?) winners.

There actually won't be one single monolithic AGI. There will be infinite variations and styles and forms.

Over time, models will become commodities like energy or aluminum. The differentiators will be the personality of your chosen AI (or AIs), craftmanship, personalization, interfaces, design choices, how multiple models are teamed up and orchestrated.

To me, that's a much more exciting future we're all working towards - and one that's also way better for users. One where creativity and craft matter more than ever.

Thanks to Peter H. Diamandis, Dave Blundin, and Dr. Alex Wissner-Gross for having me on! Just the tip of the iceberg of the conversation and you can check out the full episode here: https://lnkd.in/e4DVQ8Dx

text:
We just dropped what we believe is the world's largest study of AI conversations - and it found that what you talk to AI about actually has a lot to do with what time it is.

Researchers across both the Microsoft AI Futures team and Data Science team analyzed 37.5M de-identified conversations from between January and September in Copilot and looked for patterns in not just what people talked about, but when. They found 3 different trends by day, time of day, and time of year - and 1 rock solid constant.

1. The one thing on users' minds around the clock: health. When we ranked what topics people were talking to Copilot about, for mobile users health was #1 no matter what day, month, or time it was. This is a huge responsibility for us, and one we're super focused on.

2. Day of the week: They did find some big swaps between weekday and weekend trending topics. Gaming had a two day spike every week on Saturday and Sunday, while most coding-related conversations happened between Monday and Friday.

3. Time of day: We've all had those existential musings in the middle of the night - and that shows up in the data, with philosophical conversations increasing in the early hours of the morning. On the other hand, we saw upticks in travel-focused conversations happening most often during commute hours, with people daydreaming about where they'd rather be.

4. Time of year: Seasonal differences also affected trending topics - for example, in February, relationship-related conversations spiked on Valentine's Day. And interestingly, "Personal growth and wellness" related conversations surged over the 2-3 days before with people seeming to focus inward.

Zooming out, what the data means to me is people are truly turning to Copilot as a companion. Not just a specific type of tool, but a sounding board and support across all these different moments that make up our lives - from existential overthinking at 2 am to when you're stuck on a certain video game level over the weekend.

Studying these patterns is about understanding what matters most to our users - and where we can help. What's important when using desktop vs. mobile? How should Copilot adapt to you throughout the week? What features would help support people in these day-to-day rhythms, what topics should be our biggest priorities? It's fascinating stuff, and this is how we make AI more useful, for more people, more often.

Big kudos to Beatriz Costa Gomes, Sophia Chen, Connie Hsueh, Deborah Morgan, Philipp Schoenegger, Yash Shah, Sam Way, Yuki Zhu, Timothé Adeline, Michael Bhaskar, and Seth Spielman across both the MAI Futures team and Data Science team for pulling this together.

More in the blog today: https://lnkd.in/eXnK6gCq 
And for those really wanting to dive into the data, roll up your sleeves and check out the full research paper: https://lnkd.in/esjYhNCY

text:
Feels like there's a huge misconception out there about resilience. The most resilient people I know aren’t the most stubborn. They’re the most adaptable.

Easy to misattribute resilience as stubbornness or rigidity. Nope. Resilience is trying again, not refusing to change.

What I'm listening for in interviews isn't stories about toughing it out and staying to your pre-determined course no matter what. Tell me about when you had to summon the courage to pivot. When you had to try a different door to get to your goal.

If you hit a wall, get a ladder, dig under it, go around, build a hot air balloon. Don't keep just running into it.

You don't have to be right the first time or 100% of the time. But you do have to be willing to rethink.

text:
‘Is AI about to replace humans?’

Short answer: Not anytime soon

To match a single human brain using today’s AI approaches, you’d need something close to a football-field-sized data centre running flat out - just to mimic how one person sees, thinks, learns, and decides in real time.

All that to replicate what your brain does on 20 watts.

If you go further and try to replicate the brain 𝘣𝘪𝘰𝘭𝘰𝘨𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺- neurons, synapses, chemistry, plasticity - you’re no longer talking about a data center.

Theoretically, it can be done but you need a computer the size of planet Earth 🌍

That’s the gap people forget 🤷

AI is exceptional at automation, repetition, and pattern extraction at scale.
But judgment, creativity, context, taste, and knowing when 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘢𝘤𝘵 aren’t just more parameters.

They’ve evolved over millions of years & are emergent properties of a system that learns continuously, reasons across domains, and compresses reality with extreme efficiency.

Until we see a fundamental shift in how intelligence is computed - not just bigger models and more GPUs - replacing human creativity isn’t a near-term threat.

The real miracle of the brain isn’t intelligence.

It’s all the complexity that fits inside your skull, runs on sugar and oxygen, and dissipates less heat than a light bulb.

That’s the human flex AI can’t replicate 😅

text:
The most overrated asset in 2025 is a large language model 🤦🏽‍♂️

Everyone is talking about LLMs. It’s the new buzzword coz we think technology is a magic wand. We mistake the tool for the business.

Don't get me wrong, the tech is fundamental. But it's getting commoditized now. 

You can buy it, rent it, or build a decent version quickly. The moment something is widely available, it stops being a competitive edge.

The real money is never made in the commoditized tool. It's made in the relentless application of that tool to solve a deeply boring, high-friction, real-world problem. We are drowning in brilliant solutions looking for problems.

When I look at a pitch, I don't care about the model architecture. I look for the founder who is maniacally focused on the grind, not the glamour.

Value is not in chasing the Gen AI trend. It lies in building an Execution AI company.

𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭'𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐒.𝐄.𝐗.𝐘. 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 -

𝐒 - Solving Problems (real ones) 
𝐄 - Execution Powerhouse (brutal efficiency)

text:
What makes a great ad?

I’ve been a student of marketing for as long as I’ve been building businesses.

Over the years, I’ve created and released more ad campaigns than I can count — some good, some forgettable, and a few that truly hit a nerve.

In my view, great ads come down to 3 things - 

1. An insight everyone feels, but no one quite says out loud.

Something that captures the Zeitgeist.
In this case - we spend fortunes on weddings… but are we choosing the right life partner?

A truth hiding in plain sight 👀

2. A surprising twist that breaks the scroll.

Sometimes it’s an exaggerated moment, sometimes an absurd visual cue.
This time… an ostrich 😅

Ridiculous? Yes. Impossible? Maybe not 🙈 But it forces you to look twice — and that’s half the battle won.

3. Crafting the story through characters that relate. Something that remains enjoyable. 

If you get this right, you earn the holy grail of modern advertising.

🙏🏼 Share-worthiness 🙏🏼

We’ve tried to bring all 3 together in our new Shaadi.com film.

Did we get it right? Would love your views.
